title: Generalized comodule tube algebras for boundary and domain wall defects of (2+1)D topological order
abstract: The tube algebra, which carries the structure of a $C^*$ weak Hopf algebra, is a fundamental tool for characterizing topological excitations in topological phases. In this work, we generalize the tube algebra framework to codimension-2 defects in $(2+1)$D gapped phases described by Turaev--Viro--Barrett--Westbury TQFTs, with particular emphasis on Levin--Wen string-net models. We show that such codimension-2 defects are described by a \emph{defect tube algebra}, which naturally carries the structure of a comodule algebra over the weak Hopf tube algebra associated with the topological excitations. Boundary and domain wall defects are then characterized by the representations of the corresponding boundary and domain wall defect tube algebras. In particular, a domain wall defect tube algebra can be regarded as a generalized Drinfeld double of the tube algebras associated with the two adjacent boundary defects. More generally, for a domain wall joining $N$ bulk phases, the associated domain wall defect tube algebra can be viewed as an $N$-tuple algebra. This perspective extends naturally to general $k$-defects, namely codimension-2 defects joining $k$ codimension-1 defects, for which the resulting generalized tube algebra carries the structure of a multicomodule algebra.
summary: This paper develops an advanced algebraic formalism to characterize topological defects, such as domain walls, in 2D gapped quantum systems. It generalizes the concept of 'tube algebras' by showing that these defects are governed by comodule algebras rather than simple Hopf structures. This provides a powerful mathematical tool for classifying and understanding exotic excitations beyond simple point defects.
main_problem: The work generalizes the tube algebra framework from characterizing bulk topological excitations to describing codimension-2 defects, such as domain walls, in (2+1)D gapped phases.
main_result: These defects are characterized by a 'defect tube algebra,' which naturally possesses the structure of a comodule algebra over the weak Hopf tube algebra associated with the bulk topological order.
method: The authors employ advanced algebraic techniques, specifically utilizing comodule algebras and multicomodule algebras to classify defect structures arising from Turaev-Viro-Barrett-Westbury TQFTs.
model_or_system: The theory applies to topological phases in (2+1)D, particularly those modeled by Levin-Wen string-net models. The focus is on the algebraic description of defects connecting multiple bulk phases.
key_observables: The representations of the defect tube algebras are used to characterize the boundary and domain wall defects.
important_parameters: Codimension of the defect (2 for domain walls), number of adjacent phases ($N$), and the underlying unitary modular tensor category ($\mathcal{Z}(\mathcal{C})$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that defects are not fusion-closed, necessitating the use of a comodule structure rather than a simple coproduct.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates how a point defect connects two domain walls described by bimodules $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{N}$, showing the surrounding tube regions.
paper_structure: The paper builds upon the known bulk theory (tube algebra as weak Hopf algebra) and extends it systematically to defects, defining the comodule structure for codimension-2 defects, and generalizing this to $N$-tuple and multicomodule algebras for higher defects.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous mathematical framework connecting abstract algebraic structures (comodule/multicomodule algebras) directly to physical concepts in condensed matter theory like topological order and defect physics, which is highly relevant for understanding emergent quantum phenomena.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The point defect (disk region) connects two domain walls described by the C|D-bimodule categories M and N, with tube regions surrounding the defect.

Figure 2. Defects corresponding to gapped boundaries, gapped domain walls, and multimodule domain walls. Fusion between defects, boundary charges, and domain wall charges occurs in one dimension, such that the direction of fusion plays a critical role.

Figure 3. General configuration of defects in a two-dimensional topological phase. A codimension-2 N-defect may connect N codimension-1 defects. By considering the tube surrounding the N-defect, one obtains the associated multicomodule defect tube algebra.

Figure 4. (a) Schematic representation of an N-defect. The central defect is attached to N domain walls labeled by bimodule categories Mi, arranged cyclically around the defect. The region between two adjacent domain walls Mi and Mi+1 is labeled by the fusion category Ci,i+1, with indices understood modulo N. (b) Fusion of two adjacent domain walls Mi−1 and Mi. Here Mi−1 carries a right Ci−1,i-module structure and Mi carries a left Ci−1,i-module structure, so the two domain walls can be fused along the intermediate fusion category Ci−1,i via Deligne tensor product, producing a Ci−2,i−1|Ci,i+1 domain wall Mi−1 ⊠Ci−1,i Mi.
